title: Paths and Types
lead: Read absolute and relative paths correctly, recognise file types with ls -l and create symbolic links (shortcuts).
objectives: You tell absolute (start with `/`) from relative paths and use the shortcuts `.`, `..` and `~`.
You read the file type from the first letter of `ls -l` (`-`, `d`, `l`, `c`, `b`).
You create a symbolic link with `ln -s` and see what it points to.

sections.title: Absolute and relative paths
body: On Linux the only way to reach a file is to give a **path**. An **absolute path** starts at the root directory (`/`) and points to the same place from anywhere: `/etc/hostname`.

A **relative path** does not start with `/` and is worked out **from the current directory**. Inside `/etc`, `hostname` is enough; in your home directory the same name fails, because no such file is there.
Check where you are with `pwd` first. The meaning of a relative path always depends on the current directory.

commands.what: Prints the absolute path of the current directory.
commands.why: So you do not work in the wrong directory.

commands.what: Changes the working directory; takes absolute or relative paths.
commands.why: Afterwards short relative paths are enough.

commands.what: Prints the contents of a file.
commands.why: To test that a path points to the right file.

sections.tip: When unsure, type the absolute path; it works from every directory.

sections.title: Special path shortcuts: . .. ~
body: `.` is the current directory, `..` the parent directory, `~` your home directory (`/home/student`). You can combine them in paths: `../config.txt`, `~/Documents/report.txt`.
Files whose name starts with `.` are **hidden**; `ls` does not show them, `ls -a` does. Every directory also lists the entries `.` and `..`.

commands.what: Moves up to the parent directory.
commands.why: Go up quickly without typing the full path.

commands.what: Lists all files including hidden ones.
commands.why: Hidden files do not appear otherwise.

sections.title: Reading file types
body: On Linux everything is a file: text, folders, devices, shortcuts. In `ls -l` output the **first letter** of the line tells the type.

`-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link, `c` character device (`/dev/null`), `b` block device (disk), `s` socket, `p` named pipe. The next nine characters are permissions (covered in later modules).

commands.what: Long listing: type, permissions, owner, size, date, name.
commands.where: To find out what something is.
commands.why: You know what it is before deleting or reading it.

commands.what: Shows detailed information and the type of a file.
commands.where: When you need the type or timestamps.
commands.why: Gives the type as a word instead of a letter.

sections.tip: Files under `/dev` are hardware interfaces, not real data; do not read them randomly with `cat`.

sections.title: Symbolic links
body: A **symbolic link** is a small shortcut file that points to another path. `ls -l` shows it with `l` and as `link -> target`. Reading the link means reading the target.
If the target is deleted or moved, the link stays behind **broken**. A relative target (`../docs/readme.txt`) is resolved **from the link's directory**, not from your current one.

commands.what: Creates a symbolic link: `ln -s TARGET LINK`.
commands.where: To reach a long path under a short name.
commands.why: You keep the file in one place without copying.

commands.what: Prints the target of a link.
commands.where: To see where a link leads.
commands.why: Just the target instead of the whole `ls -l` line.

sections.warn: Argument order for `ln -s`: TARGET first, then LINK. Swapped, you get a broken link. `ln -sf` overwrites an existing file; be careful.
sections.danger: If a link points to a directory, `rm -r link/` (with a trailing `/`) can delete the contents of the target directory. To remove the link type `rm link` and check with `ls -l` first.

t03.text: While in `/etc`, type the relative path `cat hostname`.
t03.hint: The file is in the current directory.

t04.text: Go home with `cd ~` and run `cat hostname` again. What happens and why?
t04.hint: There is no hostname file in home; expect an error.

t05.text: From `/home/student` go up one directory with `cd ..`.

t07.text: Run `ls -l /etc/hostname`. What is the first character?

t08.text: Run `ls -l /dev/null` and predict first: which letter comes first?

t09.hint: TARGET first, then the LINK name.

t10.text: Inspect the link with `ls -l ~/link.txt`. What is after the arrow (`->`)?

t11.text: What does `cat ~/link.txt` print? Predict first, then run it.

t12.text: Debug: inside `~/projects/app`, `config.txt` is not found; the file is one level up. Read it with `cat` using a relative path with `../`.

t13.text: Mini project: create `~/lab/docs` and `~/lab/bin`, write a file with `echo hello linux > ~/lab/docs/readme.txt`, and create `~/lab/bin/readme-link` as a symbolic link to it.

t14.text: Challenge: go into `~/lab/bin` and create the link `rel-link` with a **relative target** (`../docs/readme.txt`); then read it with `cat rel-link`.
t14.hint: A relative target is resolved from the link's directory.

t15.text: Ticket: the application looks for its configuration at `~/app/current/config.txt`, but the real file is in `~/releases/v2/config.txt`. Create `~/app/current` as a symbolic link to `~/releases/v2` and verify with `cat ~/app/current/config.txt`.

t16.text: Run `ls -la ~` to see hidden files too.

vm.intro: On your VM, try absolute/relative paths, look at the file types in `/dev` and create a symbolic link. All commands are harmless.

v01.title: Absolute and relative path
v01.text: Try the same file relatively, then from the wrong directory, and paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
pwd
cd /etc
pwd
cat hostname
cd ~
cat hostname
blocks.expected:
/home/student
/etc
linux-lab
cat: hostname: No such file or directory

differs: If your host is not called `linux-lab` that is fine; you see your own host name.
If `cat hostname` in home does not fail, you created a file named `hostname` there.

v02.title: Read file types
v02.text: Look at the type of a file, a directory and a device; watch the first letters.
differs: Some distributions have no `/etc/hostname`; try `/etc/os-release` instead.
A `.` or `+` after the permissions is the SELinux/ACL marker, not important.

v03.title: Create a symbolic link
v03.text: Create a file in home and a link to it, then read the link.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/practice
echo hello linux > ~/practice/notes.txt
ln -s ~/practice/notes.txt ~/practice/link.txt
ls -l ~/practice
cat ~/practice/link.txt
blocks.expected:
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 student student ... link.txt -> /home/student/practice/notes.txt
hello linux

differs: If `->` is missing or `link.txt` is red you may have swapped the arguments: TARGET first, then LINK.
On `File exists`, `~/practice/link.txt` is already there; remove it first with `rm ~/practice/link.txt`.

v04.title: Type name with stat
v04.text: Show the type as a word with `stat`, then delete the practice folder.

blocks.cmd:
stat -c '%F' /etc /etc/hostname /dev/null ~/practice/link.txt
# cleanup: look first with ls -l ~/practice, then
rm -r ~/practice
blocks.expected:
directory
regular file
character special file
symbolic link

differs: On macOS or BSD tools `-c` does not exist; this belongs on a Linux VM.
If you see `rm: cannot remove ... Is a directory`, you forgot `-r`.

q1.explain: An absolute path starts with `/` at the root and points to the same file from anywhere.

q2.q: A line in `ls -l` starts with `l`. What is it?
q2.explain: `l` means symbolic link; `-` is a regular file, `d` a directory.

q3.explain: `..` is the parent directory; from `/etc` you go up to `/`.

q4.q: What happens when the target of a symbolic link is deleted?
q4.explain: The link only stores a path; when the target disappears the link remains but is broken.

summary: Absolute paths start with `/`; relative paths are resolved from the current directory.
`.` is current, `..` parent, `~` your home directory.
The first letter of `ls -l` gives the type: `-`, `d`, `l`, `c`, `b`.
`ln -s TARGET LINK` creates a symbolic link; if the target goes away the link breaks.

glossary.meaning: Full address starting at the root directory (`/`).
Address worked out from the current directory.
Shortcut file that points to another path.
Special file under `/dev` that represents hardware.
